title: The canonical substrate: corticostriatal plasticity on SPNs

html:
Corticostriatal and thalamostriatal glutamatergic synapses onto spiny projection neurons (SPNs) constitute the dominant site of basal-ganglia learning. Three converging lines of evidence justify this emphasis. First, these synapses are the anatomical convergence point at which cortical state representations meet the dopaminergic teaching signal: the head of an SPN dendritic spine receives an asymmetric glutamatergic contact from a cortical (or, for a subset of spines, thalamic) terminal, while the neck of the same spine or the immediately adjacent dendritic shaft is contacted by a dopaminergic varicosity, providing a subcellular architecture in which the coincidence of a cortical input pattern and a dopaminergic broadcast can be evaluated at the level of a single spine 1, 2. Second, corticostriatal synapses are the only basal-ganglia synapse at which long-term plasticity has been shown to be systematically and bidirectionally gated by dopamine in a pathway-specific manner, with D1 and D2 receptor signaling controlling opposite polarities of synaptic change in direct- and indirect-pathway SPNs 3, 4. Third, causal manipulations of corticostriatal plasticity–genetic disruption of plasticity-related signaling cascades, optogenetic induction or suppression of dopamine at the moment of corticostriatal coactivation, and pathway-specific pharmacological blockade–produce learning impairments that track closely with the predictions of RL-based accounts of basal-ganglia function 5, 6, 7. The corticostriatal synapse is thus the locus where cortical "what state is the world in?" meets dopaminergic "was that action better or worse than expected?", and where the resulting conjunction is written into synaptic weight changes that update the striatal policy. A related experiment records corticostriatal synapses in vivo (Figure).

The neurons that house these synapses are themselves architecturally specialized for this integrative role. Spiny projection neurons–also termed medium spiny neurons (MSNs)–are GABAergic inhibitory neurons that constitute approximately 90-95% of all neurons in the striatum, making them the overwhelmingly dominant cell type and the sole source of striatal output 1, 8. Each SPN extends a moderately branched dendritic tree whose initially spine-free proximal segments give way, beyond the first branch point, to dendrites densely studded with dendritic spines—on the order of 5,000 spines per neuron in rodents and likely more in primates 2, 9. Each spine head receives, in the typical case, a single asymmetric glutamatergic synapse from a cortical or thalamic afferent. Cortical and non-CM/PF thalamic terminals preferentially contact spine heads, whereas terminals from the centromedian/parafascicular (CM/PF) thalamic complex contact dendritic shafts, establishing two structurally distinct routes of excitatory drive that are subject to different short-term plasticity rules: corticostriatal synapses tend to display short-term facilitation (consistent with a relatively low initial release probability and a role in sustained state-representational input), while thalamostriatal synapses from CM/PF tend to display short-term depression (consistent with a higher release probability and a role in transient salience or state-change signaling) 10, 11. Electron microscopic analysis confirms that many corticostriatal and non-CM/PF thalamic boutons are directly apposed by a dopaminergic terminal at the spine neck or adjacent shaft, placing the glutamatergic and dopaminergic inputs in immediate subcellular proximity and providing the structural substrate for dopamine’s modulatory control over glutamatergic efficacy 11, 12; this includes what have been termed "dopamine hub synapses," in which dopaminergic varicosities are physically associated with cortico- or thalamostriatal synapse 13. Individual SPNs of both direct and indirect pathways receive convergent cortical and thalamic input, with cortical input predominating in both cell types 14, 15. A related in-vivo rat study tests reinforcement timing (Figure).
